nodes.label: AI for Auto-Research: Roadmap & User Guide
nodes.author: Lingdong Kong, Xian Sun, Wei Chow, Linfeng Li, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Xuan Billy Zhang, Song Wang, Rong Li, Qing Wu, Wei Gao, Yingshuo Wang, Shaoyuan Xie, Jiachen Liu, Leigang Qu, Shijie Li, Lai Xing Ng, Benoit R. Cottereau, Ziwei Liu, Tat-Seng Chua, Wei Tsang Ooi
nodes.rationale: Comprehensive end-to-end analysis of AI across complete research lifecycle organized into four phases: Creation, Writing, Validation, Dissemination.

nodes.label: Research Lifecycle Framework
nodes.rationale: Four-phase model organizing AI-assisted research: Creation (idea, literature, coding, figures), Writing (manuscript), Validation (review, rebuttal), Dissemination (posters, slides, videos, agents).

nodes.label: Human-Governed Collaboration
nodes.rationale: Most reliable deployment mode: AI reduces mechanical friction in retrieval, drafting, coding, visualization, but researchers retain responsibility for judgment, interpretation, experimental design, argumentation, accountability.

nodes.label: Artifact Generation vs. Verification Gap
nodes.rationale: Central finding: AI can produce research-like artifacts faster than it can verify them; artifact generation consistently outpaces scientific verification across all lifecycle stages.

nodes.label: Capability Boundaries in AI Research
nodes.rationale: Sharp stage-dependent boundary: AI excels at structured, retrieval-grounded, tool-mediated tasks but remains fragile for open-ended research, novelty assessment, and scientific judgment.

nodes.label: Ideation-Execution Gap
nodes.rationale: Ideas scoring well before implementation degrade substantially after execution (Δ = -1.98 vs -0.63 for human ideas); novelty-feasibility tradeoff remains unresolved.

nodes.label: Citation Fidelity Problem
nodes.rationale: Hallucination has shifted from obvious fabrication to subtle misgrounding; generated claims may appear well-cited while not being faithfully supported; top-1 citation accuracy remains limited.

nodes.label: Semantic Correctness in Code Generation
nodes.rationale: Generated code may execute successfully while implementing wrong algorithm; 58.6% of errors in research code are semantic; sharpest capability boundary at 76% vs 37-39% on novel research code.

nodes.label: Visual Plausibility vs. Scientific Accuracy
nodes.rationale: AI-generated figures may look professional while containing incorrect labels, misleading layouts, invalid numerical relationships, or domain-specific notation errors.

nodes.label: Fluent Writing Concealing Weak Reasoning
nodes.rationale: Central failure mode: text that is fluent, well-structured, and citation-like yet insufficiently grounded in evidence or scientific judgment; valley of mediocrity in paper generation.

nodes.label: AI Review Leniency Bias
nodes.rationale: Standalone AI-generated reviews assign inflated scores (AI 6.86 vs human 5.70); misclassify 95.8% of rejected papers as acceptable; strongest deployment is LLM feedback on human reviews.

nodes.label: Rebuttal-Experiment Loop Gap
nodes.rationale: Current systems cannot reliably generate new experimental evidence in response to reviewer requests; S7 (Rebuttal) → S3 (Coding) feedback loop remains major unautomated gap.

nodes.label: Paper2X Fidelity Risk
nodes.rationale: Dissemination artifacts often circulate independently of paper; polished poster, slide, video, or thread can misrepresent contribution if omitting caveats, changing baselines, or exaggerating results.

nodes.label: Governance Over Detection Paradigm
nodes.rationale: AI use in research is becoming governance problem not detection problem; detection tools have unacceptable false-positive rates; shift from 'detect' to 'declare' policies necessary.

nodes.label: Layered Architectures for Research Systems
nodes.rationale: Effective systems increasingly rely on layered architectures combining exploration, tool-based execution, and verification; orchestration, provenance, and feedback design as important as model scale.

nodes.label: Prompt Engineering
nodes.rationale: Methodological family: direct prompting, chain-of-thought, role assignment, structured templates, rubric-based instructions; requires no training but sensitive to wording and lacks persistent grounding.

nodes.label: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
nodes.rationale: Methodological family: grounds outputs in external sources including paper corpora, citation graphs, code repositories, benchmark records; reduces hallucination but doesn't ensure correctness or version consistency.

nodes.label: Training-Free Agentic Methods
nodes.rationale: Methodological family: extends LLMs with planning, tool use, memory, self-reflection, iterative execution; central to deep literature exploration, code debugging, experiment orchestration; main risk is error propagation.

nodes.label: Training-Based Methods
nodes.rationale: Methodological family: specializes models for stage-specific distributions via supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, preference optimization, RL; improves consistency and domain vocabulary but depends on data quality.

nodes.label: Hybrid Approaches
nodes.rationale: Methodological family: combines multiple families into integrated systems; increasingly dominant because research workflows require generation and grounding, autonomy and verification, flexible reasoning with specialization.

nodes.label: Stage 1: Idea Generation
nodes.rationale: Generating, refining, and evaluating research hypotheses; techniques include direct LLM prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge-graph reasoning, multi-agent collaboration.

nodes.label: Stage 2: Literature Review
nodes.rationale: Retrieving, synthesizing, and organizing prior work; spans semantic retrieval, citation-graph traversal, survey generation, deep research agents that iteratively explore literature.

nodes.label: Stage 3: Coding & Experiments
nodes.rationale: Translating ideas into executable code, running experiments, analyzing results; includes code generation, paper-to-code translation, autonomous experiment orchestration, result interpretation.

nodes.label: Stage 4: Tables & Figures
nodes.rationale: Constructing method diagrams, result plots, comparison tables, mathematical formulas, algorithmic illustrations; transforms raw outputs and conceptual designs into structured scientific representations.

nodes.label: Stage 5: Paper Writing
nodes.rationale: Drafting, editing, polishing, and structuring academic manuscripts; AI assistance ranges from grammar correction to section-level drafting and full-paper generation.

nodes.label: Stage 6: Peer Review
nodes.rationale: Generating structured reviews, matching reviewers to manuscripts, assessing review quality, supporting meta-review decisions; aims to assist rather than replace community evaluation.

nodes.label: Stage 7: Rebuttal & Revision
nodes.rationale: Analyzing reviewer comments, identifying required evidence, drafting responses, supporting manuscript revision; connects external critique with additional analysis and experimental follow-up.

nodes.label: Stage 8: Dissemination (Paper2X)
nodes.rationale: Converting papers into posters, slides, videos, project pages, demos, social media content; each format targets different audience and requires distinct design choices and fidelity constraints.

nodes.label: Artifact Generation Outpaces Scientific Verification
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting finding: across stages, AI can produce plausible outputs faster than it can prove they are correct, faithful, or meaningful; generation consistently outpaces verification.

nodes.label: Human-Governed Collaboration Most Reliable
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting finding: most reliable deployment mode is human-governed collaboration rather than full autonomy; AI reduces mechanical friction but researchers retain responsibility for judgment and accountability.

nodes.label: Capability Boundaries in Open-Ended Tasks
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting finding: AI capability strongest when tasks structured, grounded, externally checkable; drops sharply for open-ended research requiring novelty, implicit domain knowledge, long-horizon reasoning.

nodes.label: Effective Systems Converge on Layered Architectures
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting finding: effective systems increasingly rely on layered architectures combining exploration, tool-based execution, verification; orchestration and feedback design as important as model scale.

nodes.label: AI Use is Governance Problem Not Detection Problem
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting finding: as AI assistance becomes routine, key questions are disclosure, attribution, responsibility, whether scientific integrity preserved; detection tools unreliable.

nodes.label: Faithfulness Across Phase Boundaries
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: errors introduced early can be amplified downstream; need mechanisms to preserve evidence and provenance across Creation, Writing, Validation, Dissemination phases.

nodes.label: Scientific Judgment and Novelty Assessment
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: AI systems struggle with scientific judgment and reliable novelty assessment; LLM-as-Judge can reward apparent rather than genuine innovation.

nodes.label: Verification, Reproducibility, and Accountability
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: need robust mechanisms for verifying claims, reproducing results, and establishing accountability when AI systems generate research artifacts.

nodes.label: Citation, Versioning, and Source Provenance
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: need clear mechanisms for tracking sources, versions, and provenance of AI-generated or AI-assisted research artifacts across lifecycle.

nodes.label: Governance, Disclosure, and Research Integrity
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: need community standards for disclosure of AI use, attribution of contributions, and preservation of research integrity in AI-assisted workflows.

nodes.label: Cross-Domain Generalization and Infrastructure Access
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: most systems target ML/NLP; cross-domain synthesis in chemistry, biology, physics remains largely untested and likely requires domain-specific infrastructure.

nodes.label: Human Expertise and Cognitive Ownership
nodes.rationale: Open challenge: need to preserve human expertise, understanding, and cognitive ownership in research workflows increasingly mediated by AI systems.

nodes.label: AI-Assisted Research Lifecycle Survey
nodes.author: Multiple authors (survey)
nodes.rationale: Comprehensive survey organizing AI-assisted research across eight stages grouped into four epistemological phases: Creation (ideation, literature review, coding/experiments, figures/tables), Writing (paper writing), Validation (peer review, rebuttal/revision), and Dissemination (Paper2X). Central finding: AI systems excel at artifact generation but struggle with verification and maintaining fidelity across phase boundaries.

nodes.label: Artifact Generation vs. Scientific Verification Gap
nodes.rationale: Cross-cutting insight from lifecycle analysis: AI systems are better at producing research-like artifacts than at verifying their scientific validity. Ideas degrade after execution, code runs but implements wrong algorithms, figures look polished while misrepresenting data, prose is fluent but lacks depth. This gap appears across all eight stages and is the central bottleneck for reliable AI-assisted research.

nodes.label: Phase Boundary Failures in Research Lifecycle
nodes.rationale: Most consequential failures in AI-assisted research occur not within single stages but at transitions between them: ideas weaken after implementation, retrieved evidence is misrepresented in writing, experimental results are summarized into unsupported claims, rebuttal promises are unfulfilled, dissemination artifacts overstate contributions. Future systems must treat phase handoffs as explicit verification checkpoints with traceable provenance.

nodes.label: Human-Governed Collaboration as Most Reliable Deployment
nodes.rationale: Strongest deployment pattern across research lifecycle stages: not full autonomy but human-governed collaboration where AI assists with mechanical tasks (drafting, retrieval, visualization) while humans retain control over judgment, interpretation, and accountability. ICLR 2025 study shows LLM feedback improved human reviews in 89% of cases without affecting acceptance rates.

nodes.label: Lifecycle-Level Evaluation Gap in AI Research Systems
nodes.rationale: No existing benchmark evaluates complete research lifecycle with human-equivalent rigor. PaperBench makes progress on replication; process-aware benchmarks emerging for literature review, coding, peer review, rebuttal, and dissemination. But no benchmark yet evaluates full chain from ideation to dissemination while preserving traceability across artifacts. This gap is central: systems may appear strong within individual stages while failing to maintain scientific fidelity across research process.

nodes.label: AI Governance as Disclosure and Accountability, Not Detection
nodes.rationale: AI use in research is already embedded in ecosystem (17.5% of CS abstracts, 13.5% of biomedical abstracts show AI modification). Detection-based enforcement unreliable; community should shift toward disclosure, attribution, and accountability. Central governance principle: authors remain responsible for claims, citations, experiments, rebuttal commitments, and public summaries regardless of AI tool contribution. Venues need policies distinguishing low-risk assistance from high-risk substitution.

nodes.label: Capability Boundaries in Open-Ended Research Tasks
nodes.rationale: Sharpest capability boundaries appear when tasks become novel, underspecified, or long-horizon. Systems perform well on structured tasks with clear feedback (software issue resolution, grammar correction, plotting) but drop sharply on novel research-code tasks (~37–39% ceiling on dedicated benchmarks). Failures share common structure: success depends on implicit domain knowledge, causal reasoning, long-horizon feedback, and expert judgment—not pattern matching alone.

nodes.label: Layered Architectures: Exploration, Execution, Verification
nodes.rationale: Most capable systems combine three layers: (1) exploration layer searches over hypotheses, papers, code variants, response plans; (2) execution layer interacts with tools (retrieval, code interpreters, experiment runners, editors); (3) verification layer checks grounding, correctness, usefulness through execution feedback, citation validation, critique, reviewer simulation, or human review. Simple prompting insufficient; research tasks require proposing alternatives, testing, revising based on feedback, preserving state across iterations.
